questions.q: Who is the author of "लड़कनक की साईँ" and what is the literal meaning of the word 'साईँ' in the title?
questions.a:
The author is Phanishwar Nath Renu (फणीश्वरनाथ रेणु), a prominent आंचलिक कथाकार from Bihar. 'साईँ' refers to the local custom of auctioning a dead body to recover a debt owed to a landlord/moneylender.  
A wrong answer (e.g., naming Premchand or defining 'साईँ' as a funeral ritual) reveals that the student has not read the introductory note in the textbook and is confusing this story with other Hindi classics. It also shows they haven’t distinguished between a cultural custom and a religious rite.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the custom of 'साईँ' emerged in rural Bihar and what it tells us about the relationship between peasants and landlords.
questions.a:
'साईँ' emerged because peasants had no access to formal credit; they borrowed from landlords at exorbitant interest and, when unable to repay, their only collateral was the body of a deceased family member. This reflects a feudal power dynamic where the landlord controls both the economy and the dignity of the peasant, reducing even death to a financial transaction.  
A wrong answer that focuses only on "poverty" without linking it to the structural absence of banking or the landlord’s coercive power shows a superficial understanding. It misses the systemic exploitation that Renu critiques.

questions.q: A similar practice called 'मृतक नीलामी' existed in parts of eastern Uttar Pradesh where a dead body was kept as security until the debt was paid. Compare this with 'साईँ' in Bihar: identify one similarity and one difference in the social function of the two customs.
questions.a:
Similarity: Both customs treat the corpse as economic collateral, stripping the family of ritual dignity. Difference: In 'साईँ' the body is publicly auctioned to the highest bidder (often the same landlord), while in 'मृतक नीलामी' the body is retained by the creditor until repayment, making it a pawn rather than an auction.  
A wrong answer that says "they are the same" ignores the nuance of public auction vs. private pawn, which changes the public humiliation aspect central to Renu’s story. It also indicates the student cannot transfer contextual knowledge to a parallel case.

questions.q: Phanishwar Nath Renu participated in the 1942 Quit India Movement and worked as a journalist in rural Bihar. Analyze how these two experiences likely shaped his portrayal of the landlord‑peasant conflict in "लड़कनक की साईँ".
questions.a:
His involvement in the freedom struggle exposed him to the gap between political independence and persistent economic bondage, making him sensitive to the continuation of feudal exploitation. His journalism gave him first‑hand observation of dialect, rituals, and power plays, enabling authentic आंचलिक detailing (e.g., the dialogue in मैथिली‑मिश्रित हिन्दी). Together, they ensure the story is not a romanticized village sketch but a documented indictment.  
A wrong answer that merely lists his biography without connecting each experience to a specific literary choice (e.g., "he wrote realistically because he was a journalist") shows an inability to synthesize life‑experience with textual effect.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "A reader can fully appreciate 'लड़कनक की साईँ' without any knowledge of the historical context or the custom of 'साईँ' because the story’s emotions are universal." Defend your position with two textual reasons.
questions.a:
The claim is false. First, the central conflict — the auction of the corpse — is unintelligible without knowing that 'साईँ' was a real, legally unrecognized but socially enforced practice; the horror loses its specificity. Second, the dialogue and dialect (e.g., "पवैयग बाँक न किया", "नखंजिक") carry cultural codes (caste, power, resistance) that a context‑less reader would miss, flattening the characters into generic victims. Universal emotions exist, but their particular expression here is historically conditioned.  
A wrong answer that agrees with the claim reveals a "universalist" fallacy common in students who equate literature with timeless moral tales, ignoring the CBSE’s emphasis on historicizing texts.

questions.q: Create a 5‑point pre‑reading guide (bullet points) for a classmate who has never heard of Phanishwar Nath Renu or the custom of 'साईँ'. Each point must be one sentence and cover: author, region, custom, economic system, and one key vocabulary word.
questions.a:
- Phanishwar Nath Renu (1921–1977) was a Bihar‑born freedom fighter and journalist whose आंचलिक stories depict rural life with linguistic authenticity.  
- The story is set in a village in the Kosi‑Seemanchal region of Bihar, an area prone to flooding and feudal landholding.  
- 'साईँ' is a local custom where a landlord auctions a debtor’s dead body to recover loans, turning grief into a public spectacle.  
- The zamindari system and absence of rural banks forced peasants into hereditary debt bondage, making such customs feasible.  
- Key word: मिप्सरुक (mipsruk) — continuous, unending movement, used in the opening to describe the relentless cycle of poverty.  
A poor answer that lists only plot points or omits the economic system shows the student cannot distinguish context from narrative.
